_comment: Versions whose package was actually handed to the user. A build that was made
but not delivered does not belong here.
This exists because 1.6.2 was delivered twice with different contents. fa8b305
was built, verified and sent; fe581b8 then fixed three review findings and was
built and verified under the same version number. Both are 1.6.2, so the About
row in Settings shows the same number for either, and device feedback on the
three fixes could not be attributed to a build. Nothing failed at the time:
every gate compared the three in-repo version literals against each other, and
they agreed.
The gate this file feeds asks a question those checks cannot: does this version
number still identify exactly one package? Reusing a delivered number is only a
defect once the shipped bytes would differ, so the assertion is not 'never
reuse' but 'if this number was delivered, the shipping source must still be the
source it was delivered from'. That keeps the tree green immediately after a
delivery, and turns red on the first change that would alter the package, which
is when it matters. A gate that is red for ordinary reasons is a gate people
learn to ignore.
shippingDigest is therefore the load-bearing field. It comes from
scripts/shipping_digest.py, which hashes every tracked path that can change the
built package and excludes only prose, tests, and the verifiers that read a
build rather than produce one. Inclusion is the default, so a new source
directory is covered without anyone remembering to add it. A docs or test commit
therefore does not invalidate a delivered version, and a source edit does even
before it is committed, because the digest reads the working tree.
sourceSha and runId are provenance: they name where the package came from, and
are not what the gate compares.
Limitations, stated rather than waived. A delivery that is never recorded here
leaves the gate inert for that number; the forward-progress assertion is what
covers unrecorded older numbers. The digest proves the inputs match, not that
the output bytes match: the toolchain is pinned in the workflow, which is itself
inside the digest, but LC_UUID alone already makes the deb non-reproducible, so
identical inputs are the strongest available claim. The ledger starts at 1.6.1
because those are the packages whose bytes are still on hand to hash; earlier
releases are not reconstructed from memory.
sha256 is the roothide package, which is the lane that gets delivered.
